Whether or not inflation is possible in the first place hinges on the sign of $\lambda_{\rm nl}(\mu_{\rm m})$ , since $\lambda_{\rm nl}<0$ would correspond to the potential flipping over, causing the scalar field to roll towards larger field values and ultimately the Universe to crunch. In agreement with earlier investigations [32, 105, 47, 70], our analysis finds this behavior in a majority of parameter space: for the $1\sigma$ -confidence ellipsoid, we find that $99.6\%$ of the parameter-space points covered in our scan yield $\lambda_{\rm nl}(\mu_{\rm m})<0$ , including the central value. Within the $2\sigma$ - and $3\sigma$ -confidence ellipsoids, we find this behavior for $90.7\%$ and $82.5\%$ of the parameter-space points, respectively.

Earlier works [32, 62, 52, 38, 99] have pointed out that this conclusion could be dramatically altered through the effect of BSM physics capable of restoring vacuum stability. These authors have suggested to quantify such effects through the introduction of a threshold correction to the quartic coupling,

$$ \displaystyle\lambda_{\rm nl,SM}\to\lambda_{\rm nl,SM}+\Delta\lambda_{\rm nl}\equiv\lambda_{\rm nl}. $$

For the purpose of our analysis, we combine the possibility of such an effect with the SM error bars by treating the overall $\lambda_{\rm nl}$ effectively as a free parameter.44 4 Whereas in principle such BSM effects could also influence the parameters $\lambda_{\rm ll}(\mu_{\rm m})$ and $\mu_{\rm m}$ , we expect that the impact on these parameters would be less significant than on $\lambda_{\rm nl}$ , and likely comparable to the measurement uncertainties at the EW scale that we have already incorporated within our analysis. Therefore we only consider possible effects on $\lambda_{\rm nl}(\mu_{\rm m})$ in our analysis. In particular, near the critical point, we parameterize

$$ \displaystyle\lambda_{\rm nl}=\lambda_{\rm nl,crit}(1+\delta),\>\,{\rm where}\>\,\lambda_{\rm nl,crit}=\lambda_{\rm ll}/16. $$

We focus on the case $\delta>0$ , corresponding to a monotonically growing potential.

In our main analysis, EW-scale measurements will manifest through the parameters $\{\mu_{\rm m},\lambda_{\rm ll},\delta\}$ . In order to focus our scan on near-critical behavior, we will choose $0<\delta\ll 1$ , ignoring any correlation with $\mu_{\rm m}$ and $\lambda_{\rm ll}$ . For the latter, we consider a grid of 471 points obtained from a uniform $32\times 32$ rectangular grid of values overlaid on the SM $3\sigma$ -confidence region, projected into the $(\mu_{\rm m},\lambda_{\rm ll})$ plane. See Fig. 2. Throughout the remainder of this article, we will refer to this region as the SM $3\sigma$ region. Neglecting the correlation between the freely chosen perturbation away from exact criticality, $\delta$ , and the other parameters amounts to a strict extension of the relevant parameter space to include BSM scenarios or account for systematic errors, as discussed in the previous paragraph. We will show that even across this extended parameter space, models of critical Higgs inflation cannot simultaneously satisfy the three criteria enumerated in Sec. II. A fortiori, neither can the baseline model with purely SM EW input parameters.

Eq. (28) implies that near-critical behavior requires a deviation from the usual power counting of the loop expansion, in which $\lambda_{\rm nl}$ would be expected to be dominated by a tree-level part, while $\lambda_{\rm ll}$ only emerges at the two-loop level. Both in the pure SM as well as in our extension, which allows for threshold effects ( $\lambda_{\rm nl}\to\lambda_{\rm nl}+\Delta\lambda$ ), the terms $\lambda_{\rm nl}$ and $\lambda_{\rm ll}$ become comparable due to $\lambda_{\rm l}(\mu_{\rm m})\simeq 0$ , leaving $\lambda_{\rm nl}\sim{\cal O}(\text{two-loop})$ . It is then easy to see that these specific conditions do not spoil the loop expansion more generally, given that the logarithms remain sufficiently small, which is assured as long as $z=\mathcal{O}(0.1-10)$ , where $z(h)$ is defined in Eq. (21).

## V Inflationary Dynamics and Cosmological Observables

In this section we consider inflationary dynamics for models of Higgs inflation near the critical point, for both the metric and Palatini formulations of gravity.

As noted above Eq. (10), at energy scales far above the EW symmetry-breaking scale, and following a possible initial transient, the background dynamics of the multifield system evolve along an effectively single-field trajectory within field space, which we may select to be the $\phi^{0}=h$ direction. The effectively single-field dynamics persist in these models because neither $V_{E}(h)$ nor ${\cal G}_{IJ}(\phi^{I})$ include sufficiently large gradients to push the system away from evolving along the radial direction in field space. In the absence of any such turning among the background fields—at least during the final 60 e-folds of inflation—the system evolves with $\phi^{I}\sim\dot{\phi}^{I}\sim 0$ for $I\geq 1$ [63, 72, 73, 101, 76, 44].

Within the single-field attractor, the relevant component of the field-space metric in Eq. (19) is simply ${\cal G}_{hh}$ , and we may introduce a single real-valued, canonically normalized scalar field $\chi$ in the Einstein frame via the rescaling [75]

$$ \frac{d\chi}{dh}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{\cal G}_{hh}}}=\frac{M_{\rm Pl}^{2}+\xi h^{2}}{M_{\rm Pl}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{M_{\rm Pl}^{2}+\xi(1+6\sigma\xi)h^{2}}}. $$

The rescaling in Eq. (29) depends on the underlying formulation of gravity. For the metric-gravity case ( $\sigma=1$ ), Eq. (29) may be solved analytically (see, e.g., Eq. (3.7) in Ref. [104]), though during inflation, for $h\gg M_{\rm Pl}/\sqrt{\xi}$ and $\xi\gg 1$ , the solution simplifies to [23]

$$ \chi(h)\simeq\sqrt{6}\,M_{\rm Pl}\,{\rm ln}\left(\frac{\sqrt{\xi}\,h}{M_{\rm Pl}}\right)\quad{\rm(metric)}. $$

Meanwhile, in the Palatini-gravity case ( $\sigma=0$ ), Eq. (29) may be solved analytically in a simple form for arbitrary $\xi$ (see Eq. (3.16) in Ref. [104]):

$$ \chi(h)=\frac{M_{\rm Pl}}{\sqrt{\xi}}{\rm sinh}^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{\xi}\,h}{M_{\rm Pl}}\right)\quad{\rm(Palatini)}. $$

See Fig. 3 for plots of the mappings between $h$ and $\chi(h)$ for both metric and Palatini cases.

In both formulations (metric or Palatini), varying the effective action in the Einstein frame with respect to $g_{\mu\nu}$ and $\chi$ yields the coupled equations of motion,

$$ \ddot{\chi}+3H\dot{\chi}+V_{E}^{\prime}=0 $$

and

$$ \displaystyle H^{2} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{3M_{\rm Pl}^{2}}\left[\frac{1}{2}\dot{\chi}^{2}+V_{E}(\chi)\right], \displaystyle\dot{H} \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2M_{\rm Pl}^{2}}\dot{\chi}^{2}, $$

where a prime denotes $d/d\chi$ and an overdot denotes $d/dt$ , and $t$ is cosmic time. Here $H(t)\equiv\dot{a}/a$ is the Hubble parameter and $a(t)$ is the scale factor of the (spatially flat) Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) background metric.

Inflation corresponds to a phase of accelerated expansion, $\ddot{a}>0$ . This can occur when the potential energy dominates the field’s kinetic energy. The potential in near-critical Higgs inflation easily yields such dynamics, given the gentle plateau of $V_{E}(\chi)$ at large field values, as well as the near-critical point at smaller field values. See Fig. 4. We may further characterize the dynamics in terms of the slow-roll parameters

$$ \epsilon\equiv-\frac{\dot{H}}{H^{2}},\quad\eta\equiv 2\epsilon-\frac{\dot{\epsilon}}{2H\epsilon}. $$

To address the usual shortcomings of the original big bang model, inflation must persist for at least $N_{\rm total}\simeq 60$ e-folds, where $N(t)\equiv\int dt\,H$ . Inflation ends when $\epsilon(t_{\rm end})=1$ , which corresponds to $\ddot{a}(t_{\rm end})=0$ . (See, e.g., Refs. [13, 85, 64, 87, 14, 78].)

Fluctuations in the field $\chi$ source curvature perturbations, whose evolution we may analyze in terms of the quantity

$$ {\cal R}\equiv\psi+\frac{H}{\dot{\chi}}\delta\chi. $$

Here $\psi$ is the comoving scalar metric perturbation on equal-time hypersurfaces. Both $\psi$ and $\delta\chi$ are gauge-dependent; the combination ${\cal R}$ is gauge-invariant to linear order in fluctuations. (See, e.g., Ref. [74, 13, 85, 14, 78].) In the absence of any turning among the background fields, the isocurvature perturbations ${\cal S}^{I}$ (which are proportional to the fluctuations $\delta\phi^{I}$ for $I\geq 1$ ) decouple [72], and modes of comoving wavenumber $k$ of the gauge-invariant curvature perturbation evolve as

$$ \ddot{\cal R}_{k}+\left(3+4\epsilon-2\eta\right)H\dot{\cal R}_{k}+\frac{k^{2}}{a^{2}}{\cal R}_{k}=0. $$

Whenever $\eta<\frac{3}{2}+2\epsilon$ , the modes ${\cal R}_{k}$ are damped by Hubble friction and their amplitude effectively freezes once they cross outside the Hubble radius during inflation, at the time $t_{*}$ such that $k_{*}=a(t_{*})H(t_{*})$ . We consider predictions for various observables on scales near the CMB pivot scale, $k_{*}=0.05\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$ .

To compare with high-precision measurements of CMB anisotropies, we consider the dimensionless power spectrum. Within the single-field attractor, this may be written as

$$ {\cal P}_{\cal R}(k,t_{\rm end})=\frac{k^{3}}{2\pi^{2}}\left|{\cal R}_{k}(t_{\rm end})\right|^{2}. $$

For ordinary slow-roll evolution, we may consider the amplitude of the primordial power spectrum near the CMB pivot scale $k_{*}$ ,

$$ A_{s}(k_{*})\equiv{\cal P}_{\cal R}(k_{*},t_{\rm end})\simeq\frac{H^{2}(t_{*})}{8\pi M_{\rm Pl}^{2}\epsilon(t_{*})}, $$

its spectral index $n_{s}$ ,

$$ \begin{split}n_{s}(k_{*})&\equiv 1+\frac{d{\rm ln}{\cal P}_{\cal R}(k,t_{\rm end})}{d{\rm ln}k}\bigg|_{k_{*}}\\
&\simeq 1-6\epsilon(t_{*})+2\eta(t_{*}),\end{split} $$

the running of the spectral index $\alpha_{s}$ ,

$$ \alpha_{s}(k_{*})\equiv\frac{dn_{s}}{d{\rm ln}k}\bigg|_{k_{*}}\simeq\frac{\dot{n}_{s}(t_{*})}{H(t_{*})}, $$

and the tensor-to-scalar ratio $r$ ,

$$ r\equiv\frac{{\cal P}_{T}(k,t_{\rm end})}{{\cal P}_{\cal R}(k,t_{\rm end})}\bigg|_{k_{*}}\simeq 16\epsilon(t_{*}), $$

where ${\cal P}_{T}(k,t_{\rm end})$ is the dimensionless power spectrum of primordial tensor modes evaluated at the end of inflation. In Eqs. (39)–(42), the expressions given in terms of the slow-roll parameters hold when the system undergoes ordinary slow-roll evolution, with $|\epsilon|,|\eta|\ll 1$ [13]. Meanwhile, evolution within the single-field attractor suppresses typical multifield features, such as the fraction of power in isocurvature perturbations $\beta_{\rm iso}(k_{*})$ and primordial non-Gaussianity $f_{\rm NL}$ [72, 73, 101].

Modes near $k_{*}$ cross outside the Hubble radius at the time [49, 82]

$$ N_{*}\simeq 62+\frac{1}{4}{\rm ln}\left(\frac{V_{E}^{2}(t_{*})}{3M_{\rm Pl}^{6}H^{2}(t_{\rm end})}\right)-\frac{N_{\rm reh}}{4} $$

e-folds before the end of inflation. Here $N_{\rm reh}$ denotes the duration of reheating after the end of inflation [7]. Models like Higgs inflation reheat efficiently, with $N_{\rm reh}\lesssim 3$ [17, 58, 103, 44, 45, 46, 91, 106, 16, 80, 15, 56, 41], so in this work we calculate predictions for CMB observables upon evaluating $N_{*}$ in Eq. (43) for a given set of parameters (which affect $V_{E}(t_{*})$ and $H(t_{\rm end})$ ), while neglecting $N_{\rm reh}$ . Across most of parameter space of interest here, we find $N_{*}\simeq 56$ e-folds before the end of inflation.

Predictions from models of inflation can be compared with high-precision measurements of CMB anisotropies, which yield [4, 2]

$$ \begin{split}A_{s}&=\left(2.09\pm 0.10\right)\times 10^{-9},\\
n_{s}&=0.9649\pm 0.0042,\\
\alpha_{s}&=-0.0045\pm 0.0067,\\

each evaluated at the CMB pivot scale $k_{*}=0.05\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$ . Here we use the best-fit values from the Planck 2018 analysis, which remain consistent with the more recent reports from the ACT [33] and SPT [35] collaborations [55]. The small shifts in central values for quantities such as $n_{s}$ among Refs. [4, 33, 35] do not have any impact on our overall conclusions regarding critical Higgs inflation. When matching

Finally, we note that in models that include a near-inflection point, such as critical Higgs inflation, the system may depart from ordinary slow-roll evolution at some time before inflation ends. In particular, in the vicinity of the region in which $V_{E}^{\prime}(\chi)\simeq 0$ , the parameter $\epsilon\rightarrow 0^{+}$ and $\eta\rightarrow 3$ , giving rise a phase known as ultra-slow-roll evolution [79, 86, 48, 94]. Given the form of the equation of motion for modes ${\cal R}_{k}$ in Eq. (37), we see that modes of comoving $k$ for which $k\ll aH$ while $\eta>\frac{3}{2}+2\epsilon$ , during ultra-slow-roll, will be amplified. This can yield observable signatures such as enhanced gravitational waves—induced at second-order in perturbation theory by the large amplitude of ${\cal R}_{k}$ —and the production of primordial black holes soon after the end of inflation. (For reviews, see Refs. [5, 50, 53, 92].) Previous authors have indeed identified regions of parameter space in models of critical Higgs inflation in which each of these phenomena can occur [54, 24].

Given our interest in this article in the three criteria—consistency with precision EW-scale measurements, CMB observables, and limited sensitivity to unknown UV physics—it suffices in our case to consider the threshold correction factor $\delta\sim{\cal O}(10^{-2})$ . In our analysis, therefore, we never consider points in parameter space that get arbitrarily close to the actual inflection point ( $\delta=0$ ). Many previous studies have indicated that departures from ordinary slow-roll evolution in (effectively) single-field inflation, of the sort that can source detectable gravitational waves and/or primordial black holes, require fine-tuning at least one dimensionless parameter to one part in ${\cal O}(10^{4})$ or below. (See, e.g., Refs. [54, 24, 59, 60, 97, 42, 83, 84].) In the present case, by limiting attention to $\delta\sim{\cal O}(10^{-2})$ , we confirm that the system never leaves ordinary slow-roll, and hence the regions of parameter space on which we focus produce neither detectable gravitational waves nor primordial black holes.

## VI Perturbative Unitarity and sensitivity to new physics

One of the biggest conceptual appeals of Higgs inflation is the possibility to probe the inflaton field at relatively low energies. A necessary condition for establishing this connection is that the same underlying model serves as a reliable effective description across vastly different regimes—in particular, near both $\langle h\rangle=v_{\rm EW}\sim{\cal O}(10^{2}\,{\rm GeV})\ll M_{\rm Pl}$ and $\langle h\rangle\sim h_{\rm infl}\sim M_{\rm Pl}/\sqrt{\xi}$ . For ordinary, tree-level Higgs inflation, earlier investigations have shown that scattering of Higgs particles with energies larger than some cutoff $\Lambda$ would lead to a violation of perturbative unitarity [30, 31, 10, 69, 18, 61, 81, 21, 26, 34, 9, 104]. This issue arises from the relatively large values of $\xi$ necessary for predictions from tree-level Higgs inflation to match cosmological observables. The ability of near-critical Higgs inflation to yield the correct CMB observables for significantly smaller values of $\xi$ thus suggests that it might avoid these unitarity issues. In this section, we give a brief review of a recent high-precision unitarity analysis capable of capturing the near-critical regime [104], before applying these results in Sec. VII.

The violation of perturbative unitarity by the nonminimal coupling can best be understood by representing the coupling in terms of higher-dimensional operators following the conformal transformation of Eq. (16). For metric gravity with $\xi\gg 1$ , and expanding around $\langle h\rangle\sim v_{\rm EW}\ll M_{\rm Pl}/\sqrt{\xi}$ , the most important terms are the nondiagonal elements of the field-space metric ${\cal G}_{IJ}(\phi^{K})$ in Eq. (19),

$$ \begin{split}\frac{\mathcal{L}}{\sqrt{-g}}\supset&\>3\frac{\xi^{2}M_{\rm Pl}^{2}}{(M_{\rm Pl}^{2}+2\xi|\mathbf{H}|^{2})^{2}}\delta_{IK}\delta_{JL}\phi^{K}\phi^{L}\partial_{\mu}\phi^{I}\partial_{\nu}\phi^{J}\\
\simeq&\>3\frac{\xi^{2}}{M_{\rm Pl}^{2}}\delta_{IK}\delta_{JL}\phi^{K}\phi^{L}\partial_{\mu}\phi^{I}\partial_{\nu}\phi^{J},\end{split} $$

where we have neglected terms suppressed by higher powers of $M_{\rm Pl}/\sqrt{\xi}$ in the last step. In this section we will briefly consider the dominant contribution to scattering matrix elements that arises from this particular interaction; see Ref. [104] for a more complete discussion.

Eq. (VI) gives rise to a four-point interaction between different species of scalars within the Higgs doublet. Through dimensional analysis alone, it is easy to see that the corresponding S-matrix element for the scattering of two scalar particles with center-of-mass energy $E$ scales as

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{2\to 2}\sim\left(\frac{E\cdot\xi}{M_{\rm Pl}}\right)^{2}, $$

with each factor of $E$ arising from one of the derivatives in Eq. (VI). Perturbative unitarity of the S-matrix requires that $|\mathcal{M}_{2\to 2}|^{2}<1$ . Restoring the prefactors dropped in Eq. (45), this implies that the Lagrangian can only consistently be valid for energies [104]

$$ \displaystyle E<E_{\rm max}^{\rm EW}\simeq 2.05\,\frac{M_{\rm Pl}}{\xi}\quad\quad(\text{metric}). $$

Demanding perturbative unitarity therefore implies that the theory needs to be modified above some intermediate scale $\Lambda<E^{\rm EW}_{\rm max}$ in such a way that $|\mathcal{M}_{2\to 2}|^{2}$ remains smaller than $1$ . Yet any new physics, beyond the terms in Eqs. (13), (18), and (19) that could alter these scattering amplitudes could also affect the inflationary dynamics. This would render cosmological predictions from the model dependent upon the details of the UV completion [10].

A similar argument applies in the case of Higgs inflation in the Palatini formulation of gravity. As noted below Eq. (19), the Palatini case corresponds to $\sigma=0$ , so that the term in Eq. (VI) remains absent. For small $\lambda_{\rm nl}$ , the relevant scattering amplitudes in the Palatini case arise instead from terms suppressed by powers of $E/(\sqrt{\xi}\,M_{\rm Pl})$ . In Ref. [104], it was shown that this leads to an upper bound

$$ \displaystyle E<E_{\rm max}^{\rm EW}\simeq 4.94\,\frac{M_{\rm Pl}}{\sqrt{\xi}}\quad\quad(\text{Palatini}). $$

Although the scaling of $E_{\rm max}^{\rm EW}$ with $\xi$ is parametrically weaker for the Palatini case compared to the metric-gravity case, we will see in Sec. VII that successful inflation in the Palatini case typically requires much larger values of $\xi$ . We must therefore consider perturbative unitarity carefully for each model.

Before applying these results to near-critical Higgs inflation, it is important to note two conceptual subtleties. First, the results in Eqs. (46) and (47) were obtained by considering the scattering of high-energy Higgs particles in a Minkowski background, in the vicinity of $\langle h\rangle\sim v_{\rm EW}$ , rather than around the inflationary condensate $\langle h\rangle\sim h_{\rm infl}\sim M_{\rm Pl}/\sqrt{\xi}$ . The regime $\langle h\rangle\sim v_{\rm EW}$ is relevant to consider because a single model of Higgs inflation is supposed to provide a reliable effective description across an enormous range of scales, from $\langle h\rangle\sim v_{\rm EW}$ all the way up to $\langle h\rangle\sim h_{\rm infl}$ . If one were to require instead only that the model serve as a reliable effective description for dynamics during and immediately after cosmic inflation, for field values in the vicinity of $\langle h\rangle\sim h_{\rm infl}$ , perturbative unitarity would require new physics to enter at some scale $\Lambda\leq E_{\rm max}^{\rm infl}$ with $E_{\rm max}^{\rm infl}\gg E_{\rm max}^{\rm EW}$ , as indicated in Eq. (4). In such cases, (critical) Higgs inflation does indeed behave as a self-consistent effective theory. (See esp. Sec. 6 of Ref. [104].)

Second, in the absence of a specific UV completion, it is unclear how the BSM terms would enter the effective action. The relevant terms could be represented by a tower of higher-dimensional operators involving the magnitude of the Higgs doublet $|{\bf H}|\sim h$ , or the canonically normalized field $\chi(h)$ , or even—given the form of the effective potential in Eq. (22)—the term

$$ F(h)\equiv\frac{h}{\sqrt{1+\xi h^{2}/M_{\rm Pl}^{2}}}=z(h)\cdot\mu_{\rm m}, $$

where the dimensionless quantity $z(h)$ is defined in Eq. (21).55 5 Any attempt to describe the UV-complete theory in terms of $F(h)$ rather than $h$ or $\chi$ would be difficult, given that the kinetic term cannot be expressed in terms of this auxiliary field.

We therefore consider three proxy measures with which to assess the degree to which predictions for cosmological observables are likely to depend on the (necessary but unknown) UV physics. We optimistically set $\Lambda\simeq E_{\rm max}^{\rm EW}$ , saturating the more general requirement $\Lambda\leq E_{\rm max}^{\rm EW}$ . Then we evaluate the ratios of various measures of the field around the time when CMB-relevant perturbations cross outside the Hubble radius during inflation, at time $t_{*}$ , with $\Lambda\simeq E_{\rm max}^{\rm EW}$ :

$$ \frac{h(t_{*})}{E_{\rm max}^{\rm EW}}\>,\>\>\frac{\chi(t_{*})}{E_{\rm max}^{\rm EW}}\>,\>\>\frac{F(t_{*})}{E_{\rm max}^{\rm EW}}. $$

A minimal requirement for cosmological predictions to remain insensitive to the unknown UV physics is for any of these ratios to remain less than 1.

Such a requirement is a fairly weak proxy for the likely sensitivity to UV physics. Consider, as an example, a typical next-to-leading-order contribution to the effective potential, $C_{H}|{\bf H}|^{6}/\Lambda^{2}$ . If $\Lambda\gg|{\bf H}|\sim h$ during inflation, then the effect of this operator will be suppressed by the small ratio of these scales. Yet requiring $h(t_{*})\ll\Lambda\simeq E_{\rm max}^{\rm EW}$ may not be sufficient to render predictions for cosmological observables insensitive to this new operator. In particular, the ratio of this new term $\Delta V_{\rm UV}$ to the critical Higgs potential $V_{E}(h)$ takes the form

$$ \frac{C_{H}h^{6}/\Lambda^{2}}{\lambda_{\rm eff}h^{4}/4}\simeq\frac{4C_{H}}{\lambda_{\rm eff}}\frac{h^{2}}{(E_{\rm max}^{\rm EW})^{2}}\sim 3\cdot 10^{6}\,C_{H}\frac{h^{2}}{(E_{\rm max}^{\rm EW})^{2}}, $$

where the last step uses $\lambda_{\rm eff}\simeq\lambda_{\rm ll}/16$ near the critical point, along with the central value of $\lambda_{\rm ll}(\mu_{\rm m})$ reported in Table 1. Even if $h(t_{*})\ll E_{\rm max}^{\rm EW}$ , contributions from the UV completion could be comparable to (or considerably greater than) the SM terms unless the Wilson coefficient were exponentially small, $C_{H}\ll{\cal O}(10^{-6})$ . This highlights an important trade-off when comparing the unitarity properties of near-critical and tree-level Higgs inflation. Whereas the former may reproduce the observed CMB observables with a smaller value of nonminimal coupling $\xi$ (and hence a larger value of $E_{\rm max}^{\rm EW}$ ), this requires a two-loop-suppressed effective quartic coupling $\lambda_{\rm eff}$ , thus making the potential more sensitive to contributions from the UV completion.

Nonetheless, in the absence of a specific UV completion that would preserve perturbative unitarity at high energies, we consider the three proxies identified in Eq. (49). In Sec. VII we consider each of these proxies for both the metric and Palatini formulations of critical Higgs inflation.

## VII Numerical Analysis

### VII.1 Numerical Methods

Our goal is to discover whether any part of the parameter space for (near-)critical Higgs inflation can simultaneously satisfy all three of the criteria described in Sec. II. We treat all points within the full SM 3 $\sigma$ -compatible region identified in Sec. IV as equally consistent with EW-scale measurements; that is, we do not weight central values over peripheral ones. For each parameter tuple $\{\lambda_{\rm ll},\mu_{\rm m},\delta\}$ within the SM 3 $\sigma$ region, we find the value of $\xi_{*}$ that reproduces the central value for ${\cal P}_{\cal R}(k_{*})=A_{s}$ while leaving $n_{s},\alpha_{s},r$ within $2\sigma$ of their observed values, as reported in Eq. (44).

We proceed in two stages: first, we evaluate $A_{s}(\xi)$ on a coarse logarithmic grid by solving the background field equations at each point on the grid. We identify all sign changes of the residual $r=A_{s}(\xi)-A_{s}^{\rm obs}$ and bracket each sign change, then refine each bracketed region to home in on the value of $\xi_{*}$ at which $r=0$ using Brent’s method. This procedure is described in considerably more detail in Appendix D. (The residual $r$ should not be confused with the tensor-to-scalar ratio $r(k_{*})$ .) There will be at least one and at most three such roots for any given tuple $\{\lambda_{\rm ll},\mu_{\rm m},\delta\}$ . We find that typically at least one root yields predictions for all CMB observables that fall within $2\sigma$ of the best-fit values in Eq. (44). In every case, we select the smallest CMB-compatible root $\xi_{*}$ , so as to yield the largest allowable value of $\Lambda=E_{\rm max}^{\rm EW}$ , thereby minimizing the likely dependence of model predictions on unknown UV physics, as parameterized by the quantities $h_{*}/\Lambda,\chi_{*}/\Lambda$ , and $F(h_{*})/\Lambda$ of Eq. (49).

In contrast, the shape of $V_{E}(h)$ , and hence the predictions for CMB observables, varies nonlinearly with the scale $\mu_{\rm m}$ . In the critical limit $\delta=0$ , the location of the inflection point is given by $z_{\rm crit}=e^{-1/4}$ . Inverting Eq. (21) gives

- (i) $\mu_{\rm m}\ll M_{\rm Pl}/\sqrt{\xi}$ : the inflection point occurs at small values of the canonical field $\chi$ , and occurs toward the end of inflation, thus is distant from the large-field plateau and from the field value $\chi_{*}$ at which the CMB pivot scale exits the Hubble radius. In this regime, the dynamics near the inflection point only matter within the final few e-folds of inflation and only amplify the power spectrum of primordial curvature perturbations on length scales exponentially shorter than the CMB pivot scale. All CMB observables remain well within $2\sigma$ of their observed central values.

- (ii) $\mu_{\rm m}\sim M_{\rm Pl}/\sqrt{\xi}$ : the inflection point occurs near the field value $\chi_{*}$ at which CMB-relevant perturbations exit the Hubble radius. In this regime, the resulting feature in $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{R}}(k)$ can enter the observable window, giving rise to a nonmonotonic dependence of $A_{s}(k_{*})$ on $\xi$ . For a fixed combination $\{\lambda_{\rm ll},\mu_{\rm m},\delta\}$ , the condition $A_{s}(k_{*})=A_{s}^{\rm obs}$ may therefore admit three distinct roots in $\xi$ . The middle root typically places the feature sufficiently close to the CMB pivot scale to drive $n_{s}$ , and in some cases $r$ , out of compliance with observational constraints. The remaining roots correspond to trajectories for which the feature is displaced from the CMB pivot scale; at least one of these roots yields predictions for the full set of CMB observables that remain within the observational bounds. We identify all such roots using the procedure described in Appendix D and retain the smallest CMB-compatible value of $\xi$ .

- (iii) $\mu_{\rm m}\gg M_{\rm Pl}/\sqrt{\xi}$ : the inflection point occurs at field values $\chi\gg\chi_{*}$ , and does not affect predictions for CMB observables.

The fact that the shape of the potential—and hence the dynamics during inflation—depends on the scale $\mu_{\rm m}$ in complicated ways means that the relationship between model parameters and predictions for CMB observables is more complicated in critical Higgs inflation than in ordinary (tree-level) Higgs inflation. In the presence of loop corrections and a possible inflection point in the potential, values of parameters $\{\lambda_{\rm nl},\xi\}$ that would have yielded a close match to CMB observables in the tree-level case do not necessarily provide compliance with CMB measurements in the loop-corrected case.

As we demonstrate in Secs. VII.3 and VII.4, in both the metric-gravity and Palatini-gravity formulations, one may adjust model parameters for critical Higgs inflation to satisfy at most two of three criteria: compliance with EW-scale measurements, consistency with CMB observations, and consistency with various unitarity proxies. In no cases do there exist points in parameter space for which critical Higgs inflation can satisfy all three criteria.

$$ \xi_{\rm tree,Palatini}\sim{\cal O}(10^{5})\times\left(\frac{\lambda_{\rm eff}}{10^{-5}}\right) $$

$$ \xi_{\rm tree,metric}\sim{\cal O}(10^{2})\times\left(\frac{\lambda_{\rm eff}}{10^{-5}}\right)^{1/2} $$

for the metric case [100, 104].

This difference becomes magnified in the case of critical Higgs inflation, for which $\lambda_{\rm eff}$ receives contributions from the two-loop corrections. Near the critical point, the effective potential in the Einstein frame behaves as in Eq. (22), with

$$ \lambda_{\rm eff}=\lambda_{\rm nl}+\lambda_{\rm ll}\,{\rm ln}^{2}[z(h)], $$

Near-criticality requires $\lambda_{\rm nl}\simeq\lambda_{\rm ll}/16$ , such that ${\rm ln}[z(h_{*})]=\mathcal{O}(1)$ is sufficient for $\lambda_{\rm eff}$ to be dominated by its two-loop contribution. Near-criticality does not affect the power-counting of higher orders in the loop expansion, which remain suppressed by additional powers of the SM couplings and the usual loop factor of $(4\pi)^{-2}$ . This, in turn, means that for given values of $\{\lambda_{\rm ll},\mu_{\rm m},\delta\}$ , the effective coupling $\lambda_{\rm eff}$ becomes much larger than in the simple, tree-level case, as shown in Fig. 10.

## VIII Discussion

We have revisited critical Higgs inflation based on three criteria: consistency with EW-scale measurements, agreement with CMB observables, and insensitivity of those predictions to the unknown physics required to restore perturbative unitarity. Within the near-critical parameter space considered here, we find no region in which all three criteria are satisfied simultaneously, in either the metric or Palatini formulation of gravity.

The first two criteria can be simultaneously satisfied. EW-scale measurements constrain the parameters $\mu_{m}$ and $\lambda_{\rm ll}$ through their RG flow, while the value of $\lambda_{\rm nl}$ is especially sensitive to small changes near criticality. We therefore allowed a threshold correction to $\lambda_{\rm nl}$ , parameterized by $\delta$ , and considered an extended region of parameter space consistent with the measured SM couplings. For each viable choice of the potential parameters, the nonminimal coupling $\xi$ can be chosen so that the predicted CMB observables agree with measurements. Thus, the difficulty we identify does not arise from an inability of the near-critical potential to support inflation or reproduce the observed scalar power spectrum.

In metric gravity, matching the CMB observables within the SM-compatible region requires $50\lesssim\xi\lesssim 400$ for the representative near-critical choice $\delta=0.01$ . These values are substantially smaller than those usually required in tree-level Higgs inflation ( $\xi\sim{\cal O}(10^{4})$ ). Nevertheless, for every corresponding parameter point in our scan, all three proxies in Eq. (49) exceed the EW-vacuum unitarity scale $E^{\rm EW}_{\rm max}=2.05\,M_{\rm Pl}/\xi$ : $F_{*}/E^{\rm EW}_{\rm max}>3$ , $h_{*}/E^{\rm EW}_{\rm max}>10$ , and $\chi_{*}/E^{\rm EW}_{\rm max}>100$ . Extending the scan to values of $\xi$ of order unity reveals CMB-compatible points with $F_{*}/\Lambda<1$ , but these lie well outside the region inferred from EW-scale measurements. Reducing $\xi$ therefore does not resolve the tension among the three criteria.

The same tension persists in Palatini gravity, for a different reason. The relation between $h$ and the canonically normalized field $\chi$ places the CMB pivot scale at much larger values of $h$ than in the metric case. Near criticality, the constant contribution $\lambda_{\rm nl}$ to the effective quartic coupling is suppressed, so the logarithmic term in Eq. (56) becomes important over the field range relevant for the CMB. Matching the observed scalar amplitude then requires $\xi\sim{\cal O}(10^{6}-10^{7})$ across the SM-compatible region examined here. At those values, the three proxies again lie above the EW-vacuum unitarity scale.

The cutoff used in Eq. (56) follows from scattering around the EW vacuum, whereas the background-dependent scale obtained by expanding around the inflationary condensate can be much higher [104]. Our comparison tests whether one effective action can connect the measured Higgs sector at EW scales to inflation without predictions becoming sensitive to additional, unspecified terms. The field ratios are proxies for that sensitivity; their values alone do not determine the effects of a particular UV completion. Indeed, the small effective quartic coupling near criticality makes the potential especially susceptible to higher-dimensional contributions, as illustrated by Eq. (50), even when a field ratio is below unity.

Critical Higgs inflation may therefore remain viable within a specified UV completion. Establishing that possibility would require identifying the new physics that restores unitarity, determining its effects on the RG flow and the effective action, and calculating the resulting inflationary observables. Such a calculation would also be necessary to assess proposed small-scale features of the primordial spectrum, including those associated with enhanced gravitational waves or primordial black holes. In the absence of that additional information, agreement with CMB measurements does not yield predictions that can be attributed to the measured SM Higgs sector alone.

## Appendix A Criticality condition

*Figure 13: The function $K(z)$ as introduced in Eq. (59). The maximum value lies at $z=e^{-1/4}$ as indicated by the intersection of the vertical dotted gray line and the horizontal red dashed line.*

In Sec. III, we found that the Higgs potential (including effects of the nonminimal coupling) can be brought to the form

$$ \displaystyle V_{E}(h,\mu_{\rm m})=\frac{1}{4} \displaystyle\left[\lambda_{\rm nl}+\lambda_{\rm ll}\cdot{\rm ln}^{2}\left(z(h)\right)\right]\cdot z^{4}(h)\cdot\mu_{\rm m}^{4}, $$

where $z(h)$ is defined in Eq. (21).

Moreover, we identified the criticality condition by considering the transition from the quantum phase corresponding to a potential that “flips over” to one in which it is monotonically rising. This distinction can be quantified through the number of extrema in the potential: ignoring the mass term, the first of these phases is characterized by a total of three local extrema, while the latter only gives rise to a single minimum at $h=0$ . In other words, these phases are characterized by the number of solutions to the equation

$$ \displaystyle 0=\frac{d}{dz}V_{E}(z)=\left[\frac{\lambda_{\rm nl}}{\lambda_{\rm ll}}+\frac{1}{2}{\rm log}(z)+{\rm log}^{2}(z)\right]\lambda_{\rm ll}\mu_{\rm m}^{4}z^{3}. $$

Note that this definition is unambiguous due to its invariance under field redefinitions, which would merely contribute a multiplicative factor. Dropping the constant factors and focusing on the non-trivial case $z\neq 0$ , this equation can be rewritten as

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\lambda_{\rm nl}}{\lambda_{\rm ll}}=-\frac{1}{2}{\rm log}(z)-{\rm log}^{2}(z)\equiv K(z). $$

This relation can easily be understood by observing that the function $K(z)$ is bounded from above for real values of $z$ , $K(z)\leq 1/16$ . Thus, for $\lambda_{\rm nl}/\lambda_{\rm ll}>1/16$ , there exists no real, non-vanishing solution for Eq. (59). If, however, $\lambda_{\rm nl}/\lambda_{\rm ll}<1/16$ , two such solutions exist. We therefore recover the criticality condition $\lambda_{\rm nl,crit}=\lambda_{\rm ll}/16$ . See Fig. 13.

Next, we can determine the position of the inflection point, which we denote as $z_{\rm crit}\equiv z(h_{\rm crit})$ . For $\lambda_{\rm nl}=\lambda_{\ell\ell}/16$ , Eq. (59) reduces to

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{16}=-\frac{1}{2}{\rm log}(z_{\rm crit})-{\rm log}^{2}(z_{\rm crit}) \displaystyle\Rightarrow{\rm log}(z_{\rm crit})=-\frac{1}{4}. $$

Thus, the inflection point forms at

$$ \displaystyle z_{\rm crit}=e^{-1/4}\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad h_{\rm crit}=\frac{\mu_{\rm m}}{\sqrt{e^{1/2}-\xi\mu_{\rm m}^{2}/M_{\rm Pl}^{2}}}. $$

## Appendix B Expressing potential parameters through RG quantities

For parameters close to a critical point, it is convenient to express the parameters in the potential of Eq. (11) in terms of the running coupling $\lambda(\mu)$ . This can be achieved by making use of the Callan-Symanzik equations for the effective potential

$$ \displaystyle 0= \displaystyle\mu\frac{d}{d\mu}V_{\rm eff}(\mu,\lambda(\mu),h(\mu)) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\left[\mu\frac{\partial}{\partial\mu}+\sum_{i}\beta_{\lambda_{i}}\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda_{i}}-\gamma h\frac{\partial}{\partial h}\right]V_{\rm eff}(\mu,\lambda,h) $$

Using the concrete expression for the potential in Eq. (11), it is straightforward to evaluate this equation at two-loop accuracy,

$$ \displaystyle 0= \displaystyle\beta_{\lambda}-\lambda_{\rm l}-\gamma\lambda_{\rm l}-4\gamma\lambda_{\rm nl} \displaystyle+\left(\beta_{\lambda_{\rm l}}-4\gamma\lambda_{\rm l}-2\lambda_{\rm ll}-2\gamma\lambda_{\rm ll}\right){\rm log}\left(\frac{h}{\mu}\right), $$

where each line needs to hold separately. Near $\mu_{\rm m}$ , for which $\lambda_{\rm l}(\mu_{\rm m})=0$ and $\lambda_{\rm nl}(\mu_{\rm m})\sim\mathcal{O}$ (two-loop), the first equation allows us to relate $\mu_{\rm m}$ to the beta function $\beta_{\lambda}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\beta_{\lambda}(\mu_{\rm m})=\lambda_{\rm l}(\mu_{\rm m})(1+\gamma(\mu_{\rm m}))+4\gamma(\mu_{\rm m})\lambda_{\rm nl}(\mu_{\rm m})\simeq 0 $$

Thus, we can indeed identify $\mu_{\rm m}$ with the RG scale at which $\lambda$ reaches its minimum. We can extract an additional relation by considering the terms $\propto{\rm log}(h/\mu)$ ,

$$ \displaystyle 0=\beta_{\lambda_{\rm l}}-4\gamma\lambda_{\rm l}-2\lambda_{\rm ll}-2\gamma\lambda_{\rm ll} $$

We can again simplify this at $\mu_{\rm m}$ , yielding a straightforward expression for $\lambda_{\rm ll}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\lambda_{\rm ll}(\mu_{\rm m})=\frac{1}{2}\beta_{\lambda_{\rm l}}(\mu_{\rm m})\simeq\frac{1}{2}\left(\mu\frac{\partial\beta_{\lambda}}{\partial\mu}\right)\bigg|_{\mu=\mu_{\rm m}}\hskip-8.53581pt\equiv\frac{1}{2}\beta_{\lambda}^{\prime}(\mu_{\rm m}). $$

In the last step, we have used Eq. (66) at two-loop level.

## Appendix C Conformal transformation in metric and Palatini formulations

In Eq. (19) we saw that conformally transforming the Jordan action leads to an Einstein-Hilbert action in which the kinetic sector differs between the metric and Palatini formulations of gravity. In particular, depending on whether one considers the connection to vary independently of the metric, one finds the induced field-space curvature in the Einstein frame to take the form

$$ \displaystyle{\cal G}_{IJ}=\frac{M_{\rm Pl}^{2}}{M_{\rm Pl}^{2}+\xi h^{2}}\left[\delta_{IJ}+6\sigma\xi^{2}\frac{\delta_{IK}\delta_{JL}\phi^{K}\phi^{L}}{M_{\rm Pl}^{2}+\xi h^{2}}\right], $$

where $\sigma=1$ in metric gravity and $\sigma=0$ in Palatini gravity, and $h^{2}=2|{\bf H}|^{2}$ .

To compute the transformed action in each scheme, we begin with the conformal transformation $\Omega^{2}(x)$ satisfying

$$ g_{\mu\nu}(x)=\Omega^{2}(x)\,\tilde{g}_{\mu\nu}, $$

from which it follows that

$$ \begin{split}g^{\mu\nu}&=\frac{1}{\Omega^{2}(x)}\tilde{g}^{\mu\nu}\\
\sqrt{-g}&=\Omega^{4}(x)\sqrt{-\tilde{g}}.\end{split} $$

To bring the gravitational portion of the action into the usual Einstein-Hilbert form, we select $\Omega(x)$ to be

$$ \displaystyle\Omega^{2}(x)=\frac{2f[h(x)]}{M_{\rm Pl}^{2}}, $$

where the nonminimal coupling function $f(h)$ is defined according to Eq. (15) as

$$ f[h(x)]=\frac{1}{2}(M_{\rm Pl}^{2}+\xi h^{2}(x)). $$

Recall from Eqs. (8) and (9) that $h^{2}=\delta_{IJ}\,\phi^{I}\phi^{J}$ .

### C.1 Metric Gravity

The action in the Jordan frame for the metric-gravity case is [75, 101]:

$$ \displaystyle S=\int d^{4}x\sqrt{-\tilde{g}}\left[f(\phi^{I})\tilde{R}-\frac{1}{2}\tilde{g}^{\mu\nu}\delta_{IJ}\,\partial_{\mu}\phi^{I}\partial_{\nu}\phi^{J}-\tilde{V}(\phi^{I})\right]. $$

For metric gravity, the connection $\Gamma^{\alpha}_{\beta\gamma}$ is taken to be a function of $g_{\mu\nu}$ and $\partial_{\alpha}g_{\mu\nu}$ . Therefore, under the conformal transformation of Eq. (70), the connection transforms as (see, e.g., Ref. [75])

$$ \Gamma^{\alpha}_{\beta\gamma}=\tilde{\Gamma}^{\alpha}_{\beta\gamma}+\frac{1}{\Omega}\Big[\delta^{\alpha}_{\beta}\nabla_{\gamma}\Omega+\delta^{\alpha}_{\gamma}\nabla_{\beta}\Omega-g_{\beta\gamma}\nabla^{\alpha}\Omega\Big], $$

and in $D$ spacetime dimensions, the Ricci scalar transforms as [75]:

$$ \begin{split}R(g)&=\frac{1}{\Omega^{2}}\left[\tilde{R}(\tilde{g})-\frac{2(D-1)}{\Omega}\widetilde{\Box}\Omega\right.\\
&\left.\quad\quad\qquad-\frac{(D-1)(D-4)}{\Omega^{2}}\tilde{g}^{\mu\nu}\tilde{\nabla}_{\mu}\Omega\tilde{\nabla}_{\nu}\Omega\right].\end{split} $$

Upon making use of Eqs. (71), (72), and (76), and performing an integration by parts, the action of Eq. (74) may be written [75]

$$ \begin{split}S=\int d^{4}x\sqrt{-g}&\left[\frac{M_{\rm pl}^{2}}{2}R(g)-\frac{3M_{\rm pl}^{2}}{\Omega^{2}}g^{\mu\nu}\nabla_{\mu}\Omega\nabla_{\nu}\Omega\right.\\
&\>\>\left.-\frac{1}{2\Omega^{2}}g^{\mu\nu}\delta_{IJ}\,\partial_{\mu}\phi^{I}\,\partial_{\nu}\phi^{J}-\frac{\tilde{V}(\phi^{I})}{\Omega^{4}}\right]\end{split} $$

for $D=4$ . Using Eq. (72) for $f(\phi^{I})$ yields

$$ \int d^{4}x\sqrt{-g}\left[\frac{M_{P}^{2}}{2}R(g)-\frac{1}{2}g^{\mu\nu}{\cal G}_{IJ}\partial_{\mu}\phi^{I}\partial_{\nu}\phi^{J}-V(\phi)\right], $$

where $V(\phi^{I})\equiv\tilde{V}(\phi^{I})/\Omega^{4}$ and ${\cal G}_{IJ}(\phi^{K})$ matches Eq. (19), with $\sigma=1$ .

### C.2 Palatini Gravity

In the Palatini formulation of gravity, we treat the metric and connection as independent variables. We again begin with the action in the Jordan frame,

$$ \displaystyle S=\int d^{4}x\sqrt{-\tilde{g}}\left[f(\phi^{I})\tilde{R}_{\rm P}-\frac{1}{2}\tilde{g}^{\mu\nu}\delta_{IJ}\,\partial_{\nu}\phi^{I}\partial_{\mu}^{J}\phi-\tilde{V}(\phi)\right]. $$

The object $\tilde{R}_{\rm P}$ is the Ricci scalar in the Palatini formulation, which obeys $\tilde{R}_{\rm P}=\tilde{g}^{\mu\nu}\tilde{R}_{\mu\nu}(\Gamma)$ , where $\tilde{R}_{\mu\nu}(\Gamma)$ is the Ricci tensor. Under the conformal transformation of Eq. (70), the Ricci tensor $\tilde{R}_{\mu\nu}(\Gamma)$ remains unchanged, while the Ricci scalar transforms as

$$ \tilde{R}_{\rm P}=\tilde{g}^{\mu\nu}\tilde{R}_{\mu\nu}(\Gamma)=\Omega^{2}g^{\mu\nu}R_{\mu\nu}(\Gamma). $$

Then the action of Eq. (79) transforms into

$$ \begin{split}S&=\int d^{4}x\frac{\sqrt{-g}}{\Omega^{4}}\,\,\Big[f(\phi)\,\Omega^{2}g^{\mu\nu}R_{\mu\nu}(\Gamma)\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad-\frac{\Omega^{2}}{2}\,g^{\mu\nu}\delta_{IJ}\,\partial_{\mu}\phi^{I}\partial_{\nu}\phi^{J}-\tilde{V}(\phi)\Big]\\
&=\int d^{4}x\sqrt{-g}\left[\frac{M_{\rm Pl}^{2}}{2}R_{\rm P}-\frac{1}{2}g^{\mu\nu}\mathcal{G}_{IJ}\partial_{\mu}\phi^{I}\partial_{\nu}\phi^{J}-V(\phi)\right],\end{split} $$

where ${\cal G}_{IJ}(\phi^{K})$ matches Eq. (19) with $\sigma=0$ .

## Appendix E Self-Consistent Calculation of $N_{\rm CMB}$ from Background Evolution

In the analysis performed and presented in the bulk of this article, we fixed the value of $N_{\rm CMB}$ , the number of e-folds prior to the end of inflation at which the CMB pivot scale first exits the Hubble radius, to be $N_{\rm CMB}=55$ . This approximation allows one to run the root-finding algorithm described in Appendix D efficiently for a relatively fine grid over a chosen $\delta$ -slice of the $3\sigma$ SM parameter space.

In principle, however, the pivot scale is identified as the time $t_{*}$ at which the comoving wavenumber $k_{*}$ first crossed out of the Hubble radius during inflation, that is, when $k_{*}=a(t_{*})H(t_{*})$ . We define $N_{\rm CMB}$ as

$$ N_{\rm CMB}=N(t_{\rm end})-N(t_{*}). $$

$N_{\rm CMB}$ is then computed as in Eq. (43), where $V_{\rm E}(t_{*})$ is the Einstein-frame potential at horizon crossing, and $H(t_{\rm end})$ is the Hubble rate at the end of inflation, fixed by $\epsilon(t_{\rm end})=1$ . $N_{\rm reh}$ absorbs the model-dependent uncertainty in the reheating history; for Higgs inflation, reheating is typically efficient with $N_{\rm reh}\lesssim 3$ e-folds [17, 58, 103, 44, 45, 46, 91, 106, 16, 80, 15, 56, 41]. In particular, the values of $V_{E}(t_{*})$ and $H(t_{\rm end})$ depend on the value of all parameters through the background trajectory, including $\xi$ . The trajectory, in turn, depends on the choice of the pivot scale: at fixed $\{\lambda_{\rm ll},\mu_{\rm m},\delta\}$ , the value of $\xi_{*}$ is found (through the finding algorithm presented in Appendix D) by requiring the slow-roll prediction for the scalar power spectrum amplitude, ${\cal P}_{\cal R}(k_{*})$ , matches the observed value at the assumed pivot $k_{*}=0.05\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$ ,

$$ A_{s}\left(\xi_{*}N_{*}\right)=A_{s}^{\rm obs}. $$

Eqs. (43) and (87) together constitute a coupled non-linear system in $\{\xi_{*},N_{*}\}$ . We solve this problem in two stages.

Self-consistency: In the first stage, we perform a simple consistency check. Self-consistency requires that

$$ N_{\rm CMB}=N(t_{\rm end})-N(\xi_{*}). $$

Assuming $N_{\rm CMB}=55$ is fixed, we use the root-finding algorithm detailed in Appendix D to find the CMB-consistent value of $\xi$ , and solve the background trajectory with the resulting full set of precision EW-scale measurements and CMB-compliant parameters. We evaluate Eq. (43) for this trajectory and compare the computed value of $N_{\rm CMB}$ to the fixed value of $55$ . If the resulting value is within a few e-folds, it is also within the uncertainty due to the reheating duration, $N_{\rm reh}\lesssim 3$ e-folds. For metric gravity, the consistency check on 58 evenly distributed points selected from the grid in Fig. 2 shows that the computed value is between $N_{\rm CMB}=[56.18,56.98]$ with a mean value of $56.67$ , thus the offset is systematic (that is, positive), always slightly underestimating the true value by a few percent, but well within the reheating uncertainty.

Picard Iteration: In the second stage, we solve this coupled system directly by Picard (fixed-point) iteration. Given a first estimate $N_{*}^{(0)}$ of the pivot scale, and parameters $\{\lambda_{\rm ll},\mu_{\rm m},\delta\}$ we use the root-finding algorithm of Appendix D to find the value $\xi_{*}^{(0)}$ for which Eq. (87) is satisfied. We then compute a trajectory from parameters $\{\lambda_{\rm ll},\mu_{\rm m},\delta,\xi_{*}^{(0)}\}$ and use it to update the pivot by solving Eq. (43):

$$ N_{\rm CMB}^{(1)}=62+\frac{1}{4}{\rm ln}\left[\frac{V_{E}^{2}(t_{*}^{(0)})}{3\,M_{\rm Pl}^{6}\,H^{2}(t_{\rm end}^{(0)})}\right]-\frac{N_{\rm reh}}{4}. $$

The updated pivot becomes the estimate for the next iteration. In general,

$$ N_{\rm CMB}^{(k+1)}=62+\frac{1}{4}{\rm ln}\left[\frac{V_{E}^{2}(t_{*}^{(k)})}{3\,M_{\rm Pl}^{6}\,H^{2}(t_{\rm end}^{(k)})}\right]-\frac{N_{\rm reh}}{4}. $$

Thus, the first stage is simply Eq. (89) of the Picard iteration. We initialize at $N_{*}^{(0)}=55$ and iterate until convergence, which we define by the condition that

$$ \left|N_{*}^{(k+1)}-N_{*}^{(k)}\right|<\varepsilon $$

for fixed tolerance $\varepsilon=0.05$ . The converged pair $\{\xi_{*},N_{*}\}$ then satisfy both Eqs. (87) and (43) simultaneously.

One might be concerned that we cannot be certain the fixed-point iteration will always converge. In fact, convergence to a unique fixed-point is ensured in this instance by the Banach fixed-point theorem. Stated for the case at hand, consider the closed interval $I\subset\mathbb{R}$ of $N_{*}$ values containing the initial guess $N_{*}^{(0)}$ and the fixed point $N_{*}^{(\rm SC)}$ , and suppose the Picard iteration map, $T:I\to I$ , is a contraction on $I$ . A contraction is a map such that there exists a constant $a$ in the unit interval such that

$$ \left|T(N_{a})-T(N_{b})\right|\leq a\left|N_{a}-N_{b}\right| $$

for all $N_{a},N_{b}$ in $I$ . In our case, it is relatively easy to show that $T$ is a contraction. The Picard-iteration is really a composition of the two steps just described. To see that $T^{\prime}$ is bounded, we evaluate $T$ across the grid over the SM $3\sigma$ region of Fig. 2, then compute $T^{\prime}$ by finite differences. We take $d\xi_{*}/dN_{*}$ , the change in the value of $\xi_{*}$ identified by the root-finder as we varied $N_{*}$ , then multiply this by $dN_{\rm CMB}/d\xi_{*}$ , the change in the value of $N_{\rm CMB}$ obtained from Eq. (43) by plugging in the trajectory for a given $\xi_{*}$ on the right-hand side. The maximum sampled $|T^{\prime}|\lesssim 10^{-2}$ , showing that $T$ is indeed a contraction.

By Banach’s theorem, $T$ then admits a unique fixed point $N_{*}^{\rm SC}$ in $I$ , that is, a point where $T(N_{*}^{\rm SC})=N_{*}^{\rm SC}$ . In practice, one cannot check either that $T(I)\subset I$ , or that $T$ is a contraction, without knowing where the fixed point is, which is what the iteration is trying to determine. The resolution is to pick the interval $I$ from an a priori well-motivated bracket that is wide enough to contain any plausible fixed point, and then verify contractivity. Our a priori interval is chosen by the self-consistency checks described as stage 1 in this appendix, which allows us to generously bracket the predicted fixed point. Even without this approximation, standard slow-roll inflation constrains the range of $N_{\rm CMB}$ to lie roughly within $40-70$ e-folds before the end of inflation, marginalizing over reheating histories in order to match the near scale-invariant power spectrum of the CMB. This interval is much wider than the $\mathcal{O}(2)$ e-fold displacement we found between $N_{*}^{(0)}=55$ and the converged $N_{*}^{\rm SC}$ in all cases.

Moreover, the Picard sequence generated from any initial guess $N_{*}^{(0)}$ in $I$ will converge to $N_{*}^{\rm SC}$ . In fact, it will converge at the rate of a geometric series,

$$ \left|N_{*}^{(k)}-N_{*}^{\rm SC}\right|\leq\frac{a^{k}}{1-a}\left|N_{*}^{(1)}-N_{*}^{(0)}\right|, $$

where $a$ is the constant defining the contraction $T$ , which we find numerically to be $\mathcal{O}(10^{-2})$ . Both conditions of the Banach fixed-point theorem are met, which guarantees a unique and self-consistent choice of $N_{\rm CMB}$ .

Metric gravity: Comparing to the simple self-consistency check for metric gravity, we find the Picard iteration converges within a maximum of 3 steps to a mean of $N_{\rm CMB}=56.63$ , matching the self-consistency method to two decimal places. The final value of $\xi$ consistent with both CMB and SM measurements differed from the naive value at fixed $N_{\rm CMB}=55$ by $1.7\%$ (median), with a spread of only $1.45\%$ , while all CMB observables change by less than $0.01\%$ .

Root-selection discontinuities in multi-root regions in metric gravity: There is one caveat to the relative stability of the CMB-compliant $\xi_{*}$ values found by Picard iteration. For some parameter points $\{\lambda_{\rm ll},\mu_{m},\delta\}$ in the SM $3\sigma$ region, the amplitude equation Eq. (87) admits multiple roots at fixed $N_{\rm CMB}=55$ , as discussed at length in Appendix D. Our selection rule picks the smallest root that yields a trajectory satisfying both SM and CMB constraints. In some rare cases, the smallest root will fail $n_{s}$ compliance at fixed $N_{\rm CMB}=55$ , and the algorithm selects the larger root, but a slightly different value $N_{\rm CMB}$ would yield a smallest root that is CMB compliant. If the Picard iteration happens to converge to a value of $N_{\rm CMB}$ for which the smallest root becomes viable, the iteration appears to produce a large shift in $\xi_{*}^{\rm SC}$ relative to the initial guess of $N_{\rm CMB}=55$ . This does not reflect a response in the underlying dynamics; rather, it points to the root-finder legitimately identifying a CMB-compliant root.

Our analysis suggests this occurs at a rate of less than $2\%$ within the SM $3\sigma$ region, and when it does, the pair $\{\xi_{*}^{\rm SC},N_{*}^{\rm SC}\}$ identified by fixed-point iteration remains the correct solution. In such cases, however, the fixed point cannot be treated as a perturbative correction to fixed $N_{\rm CMB}$ ; instead we identify all such points and treat these separately, which allows us to maintain the contractivity of the mapping on the remaining set of points.

Palatini gravity: We repeat the simple self-consistency check—that is, a single fixed-point iteration step—for Palatini gravity, and find that the resultant $N_{\rm CMB}^{(1)}$ has a mean of $51.87$ , and deviates from the fixed value ( $N_{\rm CMB}^{(0)}=55$ ) by $-5.72\%$ (median), with a spread of only $0.48\%$ . The resulting shift is $|\Delta\xi_{*}/\xi_{*}^{(1)}|\simeq 11.2\%$ (median), with a spread $[10.3\%,11.3\%]$ . The shift is thus both systematic and tightly clustered within $\sim 3$ e-folds—of order the uncertainty from reheating. The small shift and tight clustering mean that further iteration would provide only a minimal correction (less than an e-fold). We note, however, that the $\Delta\xi_{*}/\xi_{*}$ is about six times larger in Palatini gravity than in metric gravity; this is consistent with the larger shift $\Delta N$ in Palatini and with the scaling of $d{\rm ln}\xi_{*}/d{\rm ln}N_{*}$ which is twice as large in Palatini.1010 10 It is helpful to think about Eq. (87) as defining a curve in $\{N_{*},\xi_{*}\}$ space. The slope of this curve determines the response in $N_{*}$ as one changes $\xi_{*}$ . As a result of the kinetic pre-factors, in metric gravity, the curve scales as $A_{s}\simeq N_{*}^{2}/\xi_{*}^{2}$ on the plateau, while in Palatini gravity, it scales $A_{s}\simeq N_{*}^{2}/\xi_{*}$ . Once more, $n_{s},r,$ and $\alpha_{s}$ are extremely stable, with median shifts no larger than $10^{-8}$ .
